episode_title: Why Warehouse Automation Still Fails in 2026 – 5 Costly Mistakes

real_qa.q: Why does Walmart struggle with replacing humans with robots despite billions of dollars invested?
real_qa.r: The main issues stem from picking the wrong automation use cases—often those that are most visible or painful rather than those with reliable business impact. Companies tend to overestimate savings, underestimate integration costs (particularly IT integration costs, which can balloon from 10k to 100k estimates), and fail to standardize and digitize processes before automation. Additionally, treating go-live as the end rather than the beginning creates ongoing instability. As the principle states: when you automate a bad physical process, you get a bad automated process.
real_qa.requete: why Walmart robots struggle automation billion

real_qa.q: What is the biggest mistake companies make when selecting warehouse automation use cases?
real_qa.r: Companies pick automation projects either because they are driven by tech enthusiasm or because they target the most visible operational pain, rather than identifying use cases that bring the biggest reliable business and commercial impact. A typical example is truck loading and unloading—highly visible but extremely complex to automate—when simpler processes like floor-to-floor transport with higher real savings potential are overlooked. The selection should be driven by business case first, not visibility or technical excitement.
real_qa.requete: warehouse automation use case selection mistakes

real_qa.q: Why is process standardization critical before implementing warehouse automation?
real_qa.r: A bad physical process becomes a bad automated process. Before automation, processes must be standardized and digitized—including master data, SAP parameters, and planning parameters. A concrete example: if a customer has 12 different pallet setups or rack designs, they should standardize to three setups before seeking robots capable of handling all variants. Adapting processes to technology is far simpler and cheaper than adapting technology to non-standard processes.

real_qa.q: How should companies structure warehouse automation integration to avoid costly mistakes?
real_qa.r: Start with a standalone robot setup as a first project, then incrementally add integrations to ERP and MES systems. Do not begin with full end-to-end integration before the robot completes its first operational runs. A middleware approach is often preferable to either full vendor lock-in or complex multi-vendor interface management. Plan the overall automation landscape from the beginning while executing incrementally—thinking big but starting small—to avoid expensive system migrations later.

real_qa.q: What happens after warehouse automation go-live and why is it often treated incorrectly?
real_qa.r: Go-live is where the real work begins, not the end. Robots require a stabilization period of two to four weeks (or longer), and the system will never be perfectly stable or designed immediately after go-live. Companies must assign a dedicated Automation Master to own continuous improvement, solve daily issues, and coordinate with local IT, operations, manufacturing, and management. This owner must be defined at project start, not three months after go-live when problems have already mounted. Relentless optimization and ongoing stakeholder engagement are essential to success.
real_qa.requete: warehouse automation go-live stabilization continuous improvement
